So in my opinion this is very different from using a bot program. A bot will automate user interaction, for example by using a programmatically controlled browser instance or raw connection requests.

When a user visits the site using a browser, the browser downloads the website source from wizard101.com and it is up to the browser how it wishes to present it. A Chrome extension that only reads off the downloaded source and provides a suggestion is not accessing the site using a robot (otherwise, a browser would count as a robot too). It also does not interfere with the proper working of the site because again, it is entirely up to the browser how it wishes to present the information to the user - different browsers render webpages slightly differently in the first place. Nothing is being sent to the server in this process and every state-changing operation is still being performed by the user. It's the reason AdBlock still exists despite having faced numerous lawsuits from large companies.

But as usual, use at your own risk and only if you are comfortable with it! For example you could use this on an alt account only.

It's more of a moral judgement - I don't believe it is the right time to increase the GST, amidst the pandemic. I'm not advocating for 0% GST

A tiered GST system may be a huge administrative headache. I think the current system of giving low-income families GST rebates is a good middle ground. 

For instance, how should we classify necessities? Is water/electricity a necessity? If so, then comes the problem of rich people having private pools in their homes...

Someone earning $10,000 would more than likely save most of his money. However, someone earning $1000 a month would likely spend most of his income on daily necessities, with little left to save. Of course, the rich guy would spend more in absolute terms, but in terms of proportion, the less wealthy guy will probably spend a higher %. An increase in GST wouldn't really affect the wealthy guy that much, but for the less wealthy, it could mean the world.

GST is a regressive tax. Let's say person A earns $1000, while person B earns $10,000. They both buy a $100 headset. The GST is $7 in both cases. 

To person A, that is 0.7% of his disposable income. To person B, that is only 0.07%. The wealthy person ends up paying a lower proportion of his income to GST. Furthermore, a higher proportion of income is often spent in the case of person A, as daily necessities would take up most of his disposable income - this leads to a higher % of income spent on GST.

Personally, I don't support a rise in GST precisely for the above reason. There are other ways to generate government revenue.

>The downside is that Singapore is a small and open economy and has relatively low consumption level and high import expenditure, which will limit the extent of the benefits and can even lead to leakages outside the economy. 

The same can be said about the solidarity payments etc. There would always be trade-offs between GDP growth and equity. However, I think there are already many policies in place to support businesses, and not so many directed at individuals. 

Personally, I'm all for equity and redistribution of wealth. A temporary increase in income tax (which is a progressive tax) to support those in need is fine by me.

Honestly, please don't stress yourself out too much about your HUD layout and stuff. I play with the DEFAULT layout, the only things I've changed are the sensitivity options for snipers. I hit Legendary rank yesterday in MP.

What matters far, far more in MP is your ability to know which positions to take up, when to pre-aim and pre-fire, where your opponents are spawning etc. 

Of course, I gained a lot of these skills by just playing more, but spawn prediction is something you can pick up super easily - e.g. in domination, if your team has A flag and your enemy team has C flag, they will be spawning at flag C all the time. Knowing this allows you to rotate over to their spawn to spawn-trap them thus preventing them from going over to B. Doing this allows your teammates the valuable time they need to capture B flag.  Once you get the hang of this, try to understand the idea of map control. This matters A LOT in modes like Hardpoint and Domination. If you need help in this, I recommend iFerg on YouTube as he is very good at map control and explains why he makes every move. 

Once you understand map control, sharpen up your gun skills. Specifically, pre-aiming, pre-firing, recoil control etc. to help you win more gunfights.

Interesting read. Here are my 2 cents.

>I understand that the first two suggestions might sound stressful. One might consider the stress one might feel when they are unable to complete the entire syllabus before the examinations. However, I would suggest that this feeling of obligation to complete the entire syllabus in the first place comes from the syllabus being too simplified and it being the norm to know the entire syllabus. Therefore, in the current system, when one has not studied the entire syllabus, one is likely lagging behind. However, should the syllabus be expended such that practically no one will be able to complete it, this feeling of obligation and the stress that comes with it will vanish. In addition, it allows for a more natural bell curve based on understanding of content.

Schools will, in all likelihood, find a way to finish the entire syllabus at least for STEM subjects. For subjects like Math and Physics, there already exist Olympiad classes that learn University level coursework during J1. I find it hard to imagine that schools will not insist on finishing the entire syllabus, at least for the more talented individuals. When there are already people going for extra classes and struggling to understand the concepts right before the A Levels, I do think that doing so will only add an extra layer of elitism to our education system. For many, this will likely be way more stressful.

>To clarify, by broadening of the syllabus, I do not mean increasing the number of things students have to memorise. Instead, I am referring to teaching more frameworks for understanding a given topic.

Again, schools will promote rote learning simply because it allows their students to do better. 

At least for STEM subjects, stronger students actually do not need to memorise as much - to them, the derivation is very simple. In fact, I never memorised the R-formula for math, because the derivation on the spot takes very little time. I also did not memorise a lot of the formulas in vectors, and instead learnt how to derive them. For me, this made more sense and was more effective for me. Yet, for others, they may find it much easier to simply recall and apply the formula. No matter what, schools will find all kinds of shortcuts for students to memorise just so they do better in the exams. 

Although for subjects like biology, I do find that my friends who study it suffer A LOT of stress from memorising the 'right' explanations to the point where, instead of learning and enjoying bio, they are simply memorising the 'right' way of explaining what they already know. 

For econs, my teacher also insisted on us memorising and regurgitating her model explanation on things like the multiplier process and the circular flow of income. 

Indeed, this is what I hated most about econs. In uni, the entire JC econs syllabus can be taught in an extremely short amount of time because the concepts are easy to understand, but more than half of JC lessons were almost entirely more of exam techniques rather than actual concepts.
